issues.issue: The Bank is defined as "Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, N.A., or it's agent", so the term "Bank" may or may not include whatever affiliate or agent the named bank puts in its place. That matters because the lending, the trust and the collateral investment were in fact run by Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. rather than the named Minnesota entity.

The recital describes the Program as established for the Bank's "retirement plan, trust and custody clients", and could be argued to limit the operative appointment in Section 1 to accounts of that character. Copic is an insurance company, and the recital's enumeration invites an argument that the Program's ERISA/trust design controls the operative terms.

The recital says the Bank will make securities available to "selected" brokerage firms and other borrowing organizations, which can be read as a promise that the Bank screens borrowers. That reading cannot easily be squared with Section 8, under which the Participant assumes all risk of loss from Borrower defaults.

The recital states that the Program "is designed to allocate securities loans equitably among the Participants", which conflicts with Section 3, where the Bank owes only "reasonable efforts" on a queue basis and a single Borrower may be lent all of a Participant's lendable securities. A court would have to decide whether the recital's equitable-allocation premise controls or yields to the operative allocation clause.

Section 1 asserts that the custody agreements "authorize Participant to appoint an agent to lend securities from the Account", but the 1999 Custody Agreement with Norwest Bank Minnesota in the record contains no such authorization and no lending provision. The premise of the appointment therefore cannot be squared with the custody instrument it incorporates by reference.

Paragraph f lists permitted cash-collateral investments (repurchase agreements, master notes, treasuries and agencies, CDs and time deposits, bankers acceptances, commercial paper) and then adds the catch-all "and other short term money market instruments, and mutual funds holding any of the previously mentioned securities", leaving open whether longer-dated structured, asset-backed or corporate paper qualifies. The catch-all is further qualified by "subject to policy and standard guidelines established from time to time by the Bank", which the Bank may argue lets it enlarge the list unilaterally.

Paragraph f's permitted-investment list and its "safety of principal and liquidity" mandate cannot be squared with the investment policies of the vehicle the collateral was actually placed in, the Wells Fargo Collateral Investment for Term Loans Trust, whose Confidential Memorandum authorizes mortgage-backed, asset-backed, 144A and corporate notes with maturities up to five years and a 190-day weighted average maturity. A court would have to decide which document defines the permissible use of the Participant's cash collateral.

The Bank promises only "reasonable efforts to allocate loans on a security by security queue basis", with neither "reasonable efforts" nor the operation of the "queue" defined or benchmarked anywhere in the Agreement. The following sentence, permitting one Borrower to be lent all of a Participant's securities, deepens rather than resolves the standard's indeterminacy.

The section gives the Participant the right to demand termination of any loan "for any reason at any time" and recites one- and three-business-day return periods, then takes it back with "Bank will have a reasonable time ... to liquidate cash collateral investments prior to terminating the loan", with "reasonable time" undefined. If the collateral investments are illiquid, that proviso may swallow the termination right entirely.

The Participant's entitlement runs to cash dividends, stock dividends, splits, rights, conversion privileges, tender and exchange offers "and similar corporate actlons", a catch-all whose reach beyond the enumerated items is undefined. Whether an event not on the list is a "similar corporate action" giving the Participant an as-if-unloaned entitlement is left to construction.

The Bank's liability disclaimer turns on receipt of notice "on trade date from the proper party", but "the proper party" is nowhere identified in this Agreement. Who may give a valid sale notice — the Participant, its investment manager, its fiduciary, or the authorized persons listed under the Custody Agreement — is left open.

The required monthly report must include "all loan activity, Borrowers to whom loans were made and income earned", an enumeration that says nothing about the composition or valuation of the pooled cash-collateral investments made under Section 2(f). Whether "all loan activity" reaches the collateral portfolio is exactly what a Participant complaining of undisclosed collateral losses would litigate.

The 40/60 split is taken "on the net earnings from each loan", but "net earnings" is undefined and the same clause says all cash collateral is pooled, so per-loan net earnings cannot be computed on its own terms. In particular it does not say whether losses on the pooled collateral investments are netted against earnings before the Bank takes its 40%.

The first sentence puts "all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss" on the Participant while the last sentence puts on the Bank "the risk of loss arising from negligent and freudvlent operation of its Securities Lending Program", and the two cannot both be given their full scope. "Negligent and fraudulent" is also ambiguous as to whether negligence alone suffices, and "operation of its Securities Lending Program" does not say whether collateral investment is part of that operation.

Section 8's assignment of all collateral-investment loss to the Participant cannot be squared with Section 2(f), which commits the Bank to invest cash collateral only in the listed short-term instruments with safety of principal and liquidity as prime considerations. A court must decide whether Section 8 excuses losses caused by investments outside the Section 2(f) mandate.

The clause says that "upon mutual agreement, cither party may waive all or part of the Notice period", which is internally contradictory: a waiver requiring mutual agreement is not a unilateral right of either party. The sentence leaves it unclear whether one party can shorten the 60-day period and on what terms.

The clause states only that notice "shall be directed and mailed" to a Denver address, without saying when notice is effective, whether any other method suffices, or how the address is changed. That matters because Section 9 measures a 60-day termination period from written notice.

Notice must go to "Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota N.A." attention of a named individual, an entity and person whose continued existence the Agreement does not address, while the preamble's "or it's agent" and Section 13's successors clause contemplate that another Wells Fargo entity may act. Whether notice to the successor lending agent, Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., satisfies this clause is unresolved.

The headings are excluded from the construction of the Agreement, yet the sections are identified only by those garbled headings — "1k.", "1d.", a missing Section 7 and an unnumbered compensation paragraph folded under the Section 6 heading. Excluding headings leaves the boundary between Section 6 and the compensation paragraph, and the numbering of the risk-of-loss section, to be worked out from the text alone.

This Agreement and "all transactions hereunder" are governed by Minnesota law, while the Custody Agreement between the same parties for the same Account chooses Colorado law and subjects the custodied securities to Colorado insurance statutes. Because Section 1 makes the lending appointment depend on the custody arrangement, which law governs the collateral-investment dispute is contestable.

The clause binds "successors and assigns" but the preamble names Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, N.A. "or it's agent", and the lending, trusteeship and collateral investment were carried on by Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. Read together, the two leave open whether and how the successor entity took on the Bank's obligations, and the clause neither permits nor restricts assignment.

The effective date is left blank — "effective on the ___ day of January, 2001" — so the instrument fixes no date on its own words. That blank sits against the preamble's "as of the [ ]st day of January 2001" and a signature block dated 7/6/2000, leaving the commencement of the Agreement indeterminate.
